We were screaming, just acting a fool. I'm glad we can still do that,” Evette said.</p><p>Here are other tips for the weekend — from musical acts to food — according to festival regulars.</p><h3><b>What not to miss</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Headliner José Álvaro Osorio Balvín, known simply as J Balvin, is returning to Sueños on Saturday.</p><p>Balvín made history in Grant Park as the first Latino to ever headline Lollapalooza in 2019. A few years later, in 2022, he returned to Chicago with an electrifying headliner set featuring his classic songs “Mi Gente,” “Ginza” and “Loco contigo.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-780000" name="image-780000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/462f20e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5363x3010+0+536/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe0%2F13%2Fa811e0eb4de8bb6dc99886fce313%2Fsuenos-fest-052922-26.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/68fc347/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5363x3010+0+536/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe0%2F13%2Fa811e0eb4de8bb6dc99886fce313%2Fsuenos-fest-052922-26.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3ae0df1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5363x3010+0+536/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe0%2F13%2Fa811e0eb4de8bb6dc99886fce313%2Fsuenos-fest-052922-26.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="J. The regional Mexican band from San Bernardino, California, was the first artist revealed to be on this year’s lineup back in November. The band is among the next generation of musicians bringing Mexican genres like duranguense and norteño into the mainstream.</p><p>Yandel also performs on Sunday, bringing his iconic <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MepE_XoIo4A" target="_blank" ><u>“Sinfónico”</u></a> live album to the Grant Park stage. The reggaetonero, one half of the Puerto Rican duo Wisin & Yandel, will perform several of their classics with a twist: an orchestra will accompany the singer.</p><div class="Enhancement" said.</p><p>“Definitely check out the DJs,” Evette said. Last year, she wandered the festival grounds with her sister until they came across a DJ set at one of the two smaller stages.</p><p>There, they discovered DJ Drip, who is also performing at the La Plaza stage on Sunday. Evette and her sister enjoyed his set as he mixed Chicago house music and freestyle with Spanish music, she said. The sisters watched the crowd grow from about 20 people to roughly 200.</p><p>“If it wasn't for walking around and just venturing outside of the main stage, we would have completely missed it. It was just so much fun,” Evette said.</p><p>Local artists making appearances at Sueños include <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/vanguardiachi/" target="_blank" ><u>Grupo Vanguardia</u></a> and Los de la Homan, two rising Mexican regional bands, plus DJs <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/5/17/23066990/suenos-music-chicago-grant-park-jd-miriam-reggaeton-dj-balvin" target="_blank" ><u>Miriam</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/djchavaa/?hl=en" target="_blank" ><u>Chava</u></a>, <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/lemanz.oficial/?hl=en" target="_blank" ><u>LEMANZ</u></a>, <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/bompleneras/" target="_blank" ><u>Las Bompleneras</u></a> and many more.</p><p>There will also be a bachata class taking place on the La Plaza stage on Saturday afternoon, with a salsa class at the same time on Sunday.</p><h3><b>The local flavor</b></h3><p>It’s no secret that Chicago is one of the greatest food cities in the world. Much of that is thanks to the contributions of Latino immigrants operating the hundreds of restaurants, bars and food carts across the city — and there is no shortage of them at Sueños.</p><p>The La Plaza section of the festival will host about two dozen vendors. Try the different flavors of Argentine-style empanadas at <a class="Link" href="https://5411empanadas.com/" target="_blank" ><u>5411 Empanadas</u></a>, Colombian classics from <a class="Link" href="https://www.arepageorge.com/" target="_blank" ><u>ArePA George</u></a>, or tender pork shoulder from <a class="Link" href="https://carnitasoriginaldonalfredo.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Carnitas Don Alfredo</u></a>.</p><p>Belmont Cragin’s <a class="Link" href="https://poncerestaurant.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Ponce Restaurant</u></a> is a family favorite for Lorenzo and her cousins.“Definitely get Ponce for the arroz con gandules, the pincho and the alcapurria,” Valdes said. staff expect to serve hundreds of tacos throughout the busy weekend.</p><p>On the menu? Carne asada, al pastor, lengua and barbacoa. They've even hopped on the quesabirria trend and are including it in their festival lineup.</p><p>But if you aren’t craving Latin food, there's something for everyone. You can get a classic Chicago-style Italian beef sandwich from Frannie’s Beef, or chow down on some ribs from <a class="Link" href="https://rib1.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Robinson’s No. 1 Ribs</u></a>.</p><p>Attendees with GA+ tickets can enjoy burgers and fries from Bust Outs, authentic Mexican food from <a class="Link" href="https://sabrosochicago.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Sabroso! Mexican Grill</u></a><u>,</u> Baja-style fish tacos from <a class="Link" href="https://donpezfishtacos.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Don Pez</u></a>, and Puerto Rican classics from <a class="Link" href="https://orderlabombatogo.com/" target="_blank" ><u>La Bomba</u></a>.</p><h3><b>Assessing the five-year mark</b></h3><p>Sueños Music Festival bills itself as the largest Latin music festival in the Midwest.</p><p>The festival was founded by the creators of Mexico’s Baja Beach Fest, Aaron Ampudia and Chris Den Ujil, under their company La Cultura Presenta LLC. They’ve produced and run Sueños each year in collaboration with Lollapalooza producers C3 Presents (<a class="Link" href="https://www.billboard.com/music/music-news/live-nation-completes-deal-for-c3-presents-6414053/" target="_blank" ><u>acquired by Live Nation in 2014</u></a>) and Reventon Promotions.</p><p>Though year one was advertised as a reggaeton music festival, Sueños has expanded to include more regional Mexican acts, such as the popular bands Grupo Frontera and Grupo Firme.</p><p>Organizers <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2024/07/10/suenos-music-festival-organizers-agree-to-five-year-deal-with-chicago-park-district-city-hall" target="_blank" ><u>scored a five-year deal with the Chicago Park District in 2024</u></a>, ensuring the festival will continue as a Grant Park staple through at least 2029. The agreement includes an option for a five-year extension and paid attendance capped at 75,000 people per day. It also specifies that organizers must repair and restore the park grounds when the event is over.</p><p>The Park District will receive a guaranteed payment of $1.5 million or $15 to $19 per ticket, depending on which is greater, for the two-day festival. The deal includes the possibility of expanding the festival to three days, which it has yet to do.</p><p>The inaugural festival generated $120.9 million for Chicago’s economy, with $1.4 million in revenue to the parks, according to a preliminary report by AngelouEconomics and C3 Presents.</p><p>Last year, headliners Shakira and Don Omar attracted <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/suenos-music-festival/2025/05/24/suenos-festival-attendance-immigration-enforcement-music-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>more than 80,000 attendees</u></a> over two entries.title: Here are 12 farmers markets in Chicago and the suburbs worth a visit
entries.summary: <p>“Everybody deserves to eat food — delicious food, and food that isn't in the interests of profits for a select few folks who are dominating the food industry,” says Sam Koentopp, farm programs manager for Urban Growers Collective’s South Chicago Farm Stand. “It’s important to us as an organization to help people. It’s why we get up and do this work every day.”</p><p>This year, affordability and accessibility are priorities for farmers markets as they contend with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/04/27/cuts-to-snap-food-assistance-starting-may-1-worry-grocers-local-vendors" target="_blank" ><u>cuts to SNAP benefits</u></a> for customers and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/business/2026/04/04/chicago-farmers-market-season-rising-costs-inflation" target="_blank" ><u>rising gas prices and high costs for market materials</u></a>. Urban Growers Collective operates a roving bus — called the Fresh Moves Mobile Market — that delivers produce to schools, community centers, churches and health clinics in Black and brown neighborhoods. Other market managers said they are excited to bring good things to the communities they serve, including complimentary rides for seniors to and from the Oak Park Farmers’ Market and free school uniforms at the Bronzeville City Market provided by the Struggling Black Girl Magic Club.</p><p>Here are 12 markets worth a visit this season. (Check out our annual guide to 100-plus farmers <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/food-drink/2026-farmers-market-chicago-hours" >markets in Chicago</a> and the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/food-drink/2026/05/20/2026-farmers-market-guide-for-chicagos-suburbs" >neighboring suburbs</a> — updated for 2026. Did we miss your favorite market? Let us know at <a class="Link" href="mailto:farmers@wbez.org" target="_blank" ><u>farmers@wbez.org</u></a>.)</p><p><b>CITY NORTH</b></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div Winona St.<br>Wednesdays, 3-7 p.m., May 13-Oct. 21<br>Accepts Link/SNAP; dogs are welcome</p><p>Can you hear them? A ukulele group, a brass quintet and an accordion player tickling keys with classics are all headed to the Andersonville Farmers Market, now entering its 17th year. Market manager Joan Oberndorf says she thinks people come back for the connection to the community. “People come and they meet up with their friends, they see their neighbors,” she says. “And there’s a connection with the people who are growing or producing the food.” Look out, too, for build-your-own butterfly habitats and drag storytime with Bubbie Merriam Levkowitz.</p><div class="Enhancement" Leland Ave.<br>Tuesdays (7 a.m.-12 p.m., May 5-Nov. 17), Thursdays (3-7 p.m., May 7-Oct. 29)<br>Accepts Link/SNAP; dogs are welcome</p><p>“The closer you get to your ingredients, the better you’re going to eat,” says manager Jeffery Tabels. This year’s Lincoln Square Farmers Market will host Lee’s Edible Acres (heirloom tomatoes, greens and sweet corn); Dorothy’s Bakery (sourdough); and Au Levain (pastries), among many vendors. During cooking demonstrations, in a nod to the grown-at-home vibe, chefs will call out the vendors whose produce they’re using. On Thursdays, live music is on tap featuring local bands Cuban Dogs and Tijuana Hercules.</p><hr><p><b>CITY WEST</b></p><h3><b>Mercadito D’Pulgas </b></h3><p>3517 W. 18th St.<br>First Sunday of the month (noon-6 p.m., May 3-Oct. 4)<br>Dogs are welcome</p><p>New this season, Mercadito D’Pulgas arrives in North Lawndale. The brainchild of Esmirna Garcia, the founder of the Pilsen Community Market (which Mercadito D’Pulgas is replacing), the monthly Sunday market is starting its transition with a single farmer who will provide flowers, some produce, catnip and cat grass. But shoppers may delight in the market’s intriguing collection of sellers including Catrina Artesana, selling purses from Mexico made of recycled materials, and beekeepers Westside Bee Boys. A special focus of this market is pet-related goods: artisanal collars, leashes, dresses and jackets for animals, food and vaccines. While the market is outdoors, Lotz Rebel Katz Shelter, where Garcia is also board president, will host adoption events in conjunction with the market. The cat cafe inside the shelter sells tea and coffee to “help the shelter continue with its mission,” Garcia says.</p><hr><p><b>CITY CENTER </b></p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://www.southloopfarmersmarket.com/night-market-on-thursdays" target="_blank" ><b><u>City Market In Real Life</u></b></a></h3><p>835 N. Michigan Ave., 4th floor<br>Thursdays, 4-8 p.m., July 9-Sept. 24<br>Dogs are welcome</p><p>Fans of the South Loop Night Market will be relieved to hear that the market hasn’t gone away; it’s just transformed: Inside Water Tower Place, more than 100 vendors are spread throughout 50,000 square feet at the inaugural City Market In Real Life (IRL). All produce sold is “100% from farms that are within a 200 mile radius of Chicago,” says Tina Feldstein, the co-founder and market manager of City Market IRL. “Everything’s absolutely the same in terms of the farmer presentation.” There’s also ready-to-eat dinner options including tamales, handmade tacos and vegan options, as well as baked goods, olive oils, chocolates and teas. “There’s that sense of identity when they’re like, ‘this is my market,’ or when I catch somebody talking with a vendor, I realize how friendly they’ve become,” Feldstein says. Canal St.<br>Tuesdays, 11 a.m.-3 p.m., June 2-Sept. 29</p><p>Situated on a grassy oval at the foot of a high-rise, this market encourages hanging out: There are cafe tables and chairs, picnic blankets to borrow, bean bags, board games, books — basically, a cozy spot. Chalk artists sketch produce, and music is provided by live bands or a DJ playing energetic hits. Farmers “grow everything that they’re bringing to the market,” says market manager Naketa Washington. Washington recommends the brie from North Sky Farms. Say you want that brie (or anything sold at the market for that matter) but worry that it’ll get snatched up, Washington has a solution: “You can go online, you can pick the items [you want], then you can just pick them up at the market.” Pro tip: The Farmer at the Green has bathrooms with plumbing, perfect for families.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" Washington St.<br>Thursdays, 7 a.m.-2 p.m., May 21-Oct. 22<br>Accepts Link/SNAP; dogs are welcome</p><p>Gardeners of all experience levels are invited to the market’s Daley Plaza Seed Swap held on May 28 from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. to “exchange seeds, shop seedlings and connect with fellow growers,” according to the Chicago Department of Cultural Affairs and Special Events, which produces the popular annual market in the Loop. Offerings at the market’s 48th season include fresh seasonal produce, flowers, artisanal goods (natural skincare, apple cider and preserves) and prepared food (onigiri, bagels, smoothies, grilled cheese, gluten-free empanoli, panzerotti and tamales). There’s also free compost drop off.</p><hr><p><b>CITY SOUTH</b></p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://www.facebook.com/p/Bronzeville-Farmers-Market-100082943117962/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Bronzeville Farmers Market</u></b></a></h3><p>4702 S. Martin Luther King Dr.<br>Sundays, 10 a.m.-2 p.m., June 7-Sept. 27<br>Accepts Link/SNAP; dogs are welcome</p><p>If you’ve wanted to grow your own produce but don’t know where to start, stop by the Bronzeville Farmers Market. Alongside nonprofit Chicago Grows Food, they’ll be giving out seeds to give people “agency and ability to grow within their own homes,” said Elijah-Michelle Muller, the market’s coordinator. This year, the market is also will also host South Side’s Watermelon Man selling fresh watermelon; community organization Read & Run Chicago (July 19); Struggling Black Girl Magic Club, which will distribute free school uniforms on Aug. 9 (first come, first served); and resident chef Mona Baptiste cooking vegetarian recipes “at least once a month,” Muller says. Be sure to check out 11 a.m. performances from Diva Dance Bronzeville on June 6, 14 and 28 and July 12, 19 and 26.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" Carmody says there’s a pickling demonstration in the works for July. “We’ll hopefully be able to send people home with kits,” he says. entries.title: Here’s your 2026 guide to farmers markets throughout Chicago
entries.summary:
Chicago has a wealth of farmers markets, but reliable information about them can be scattered across websites and social media. To help, this guide brings together the most current information for farmers markets throughout Chicago. (We broke out 54 suburban markets into its own guide for 2026.)

This list of farmers markets in the city is organized by area, then by day of the week, Monday through Sunday, and alphabetically by market. Each listing includes the 2026 hours and dates of operation, address, links to websites and social accounts, bells and whistles (such as live music and specialty vendors beyond farm produce), and whether the Illinois Link card is accepted. A paw emoji next to the name of a market means pets — dogs on leash is the usual policy — are welcome.

(Did we miss your favorite market? Let us know at farmers@wbez.org.)

entries.title: Microplastics found in Lake Michigan, Chicago River, other Illinois waterways
entries.summary: <p>A test sampling of Lake Michigan, the Chicago River and other waterways across Illinois found tiny plastics present, posing potential threats to human health and damage to the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment" >environment</a>, according to an advocacy group.</p><p>In all, 31 test sites, including multiple samplings along Lake Michigan, showed broken down plastics present in the water. Known as microplastics, these small particles are being studied by government and academic researchers for possible links to illnesses. Plastics don’t easily break down in the environment and also threaten fish and wildlife.</p><p>Plastic food containers and bags, clothing fibers, pellets used in manufacturing and many other sources contribute to water pollution, according to a report released Thursday by Environment Illinois Research and Education Center.</p><p>Single-use plastics, “fast fashion” trends and stormwater runoff from factories using plastic pellets are among the biggest sources of water contamination, the report says.</p><p>“There is no silver bullet solution to address this pervasive problem. Multiple policy changes at the local, state and federal level are needed to combat this,” the report says.</p><p>In <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield" >Springfield</a>, lawmakers are debating a bill that would require plastics manufacturers to better control stormwater runoff that potentially releases the contaminants into water.</p><p>Illinois has taken small steps to control the pollution, including a measure signed into law in 2023 that bans polystyrene foam food containers at state buildings. Polystyrene is commonly known by the brand name Styrofoam. Some municipalities have similar laws.</p><p>Other bodies of water found to have microplastics include Calumet River, Des Plaines River, Fox River, Illinois River, Mississippi River, Ohio River, Rock River, Vermillion River, Busse Lake and Skokie Lagoons.</p><p>“While many of the waterways sampled had little to no visual litter at the point of access, our survey found that plastic is a nearly invisible constant in Illinois waters,” the report says.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2024/10/25/microbes-plastic-ludmilla-aristilde-northwestern-university-environment-research" >At this Northwestern professor’s lab, plastic-eating microbes show promise to gobble up microplastics in nature</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Lincoln Avenue's once notorious Diplomat Motel becomes stylish new shelter for the unhoused
entries.summary: <p>It used to be that if you showed up at the old Diplomat Motel over on Lincoln Avenue, you were probably in for quite a time.</p><p>What kind of time likely couldn't have been discussed in polite company.</p><p>But no longer.</p><p>The former motel, 5230 N. Lincoln Ave., — repurposed and redesigned — reopened this month as Haven on Lincoln, a transitional shelter for unhoused people.</p><p>Haven provides 37 private sleeping rooms along with on-site medical and mental healthcare, all designed to get folks back on their feet.</p><p>The facility is the city's first totally non-congregate shelter, giving each resident their own private, bathroom-equipped room. North Side Housing and Supportive Services operates a men's shelter at 7464 N. Clark St., but residents sleep two-to-a-room and share a bathroom.</p><p>The Chicago Department of Housing and Gensler architects deserve a tip of the hat for turning the two-story, hot pillow Diplomat into a bright, smart-looking facility with livable spaces that give residents a measure of comfort and privacy.</p><p>"Everyone has their own room; everyone has their own front door; everyone has their own HVAC unit," the project's architect, Gensler Senior Associate Sean McGuire, said. "The concept of having these simple [room] modules arrayed across this California motel-type circulation pattern. So, really, the framework of what is operationally best for a shelter was already there. The structure and the framework were there."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-e30000" Cornerstone Community Outreach operates the facility.</p><p>The Diplomat was one of 14 postwar motels built along Lincoln Avenue, between Foster and Devon avenues, back when the thoroughfare — which is U.S. 41 — was the city's northern gateway. </p><p>The motels were a type of California-style roadside modernism: low slung, brightly-colored with prominent, free-standing lighted signs and plenty of parking. And they were affordable. Places like the Spa Motel, 5414 N. Lincoln Ave., or the Summit at 5308 N. Lincoln Ave. There were also the Apache, the Stars, the Tip Top, the Riverside and more.</p><p>The motels started to fall from favor in the 1960s when the Interstate 94 supplanted U.S. 41 as the main North Side automobile route in and out of town.</p><p>By the 1990s, the Lincoln Avenue motels' reputations were as low as their room rates. And then-Mayor Richard M. Daley put the buildings on his hit list.</p><p>The Riverside Motel, at Peterson and Lincoln avenues, was the first to go — razed in 2000 to expand Legion Park. The Spa was wrecked for a police station. The Acres Motel, 5600 N. Lincoln Ave., got plowed up to build the Chicago Public Library's Budlong Woods branch.</p><p>But the Diplomat was among the 10 or so motels that hung on.</p><p>For all their faults, the places did provide cheap lodging for unhoused Chicagoans. Haven continues the mission.</p><p>"This isn't gentrification," McGuire said. "We're going back and we're servicing that same population, now with wraparound services."</p><p>Gensler's redo brings light, color and style to the former motel. They reclad the building, combined and reconfigured rooms and adjusted some structural elements.</p><p>The firm revived the Diplomat's original Pop Art-like color scheme — lost in a previous renovation that erased much of the building's postwar charm — and applied it to interiors, doors and outdoor furnishings, making for a cheerful, lively building.</p><p>And that good cheer gets brought to the street by way of a joyful floral mural by artist Ryan Tova Katz that adorns Haven's facade.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"> <bsp-carousel class="Carousel Enhancement" data-align-center> <a class="AnchorLink" id="gallery-560001" name="gallery-560001"></a> <div> <div class="Carousel-slides"> <div class="Carousel-slide"> <div class="CarouselSlide" > <div class="CarouselSlide-media"> <picture data-crop="large"> <source type="image/webp" width="840" height="555" srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ebc6b29/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x5413+0+51/resize/840x555!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5c%2Fc2%2Fc4d459324e019458a1aa1bdf01ef%2Fdiplomat-2605180138.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9afac39/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x5413+0+51/resize/1680x1110!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5c%2Fc2%2Fc4d459324e019458a1aa1bdf01ef%2Fdiplomat-2605180138.jpg 2x"/> <source width="840" height="555" srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/992f5be/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x5413+0+51/resize/840x555!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5c%2Fc2%2Fc4d459324e019458a1aa1bdf01ef%2Fdiplomat-2605180138.jpg"/> <img class="Image" alt="Aerial view of the former Diplomat Motel, 5230 N. Each residence features a bathroom with a shower, a wall-mounted TV, desk with a lamp and storage for clothes. Rooms also have an HVAC unit and a large window that faces outside.</p><p>Haven has a kitchen with a community dining room on its first floor, along with spaces for healthcare and social services facilities.</p><p>The all-electric building even has an array of rooftop solar panels with a battery to store energy. McGuire said the setup will keep Haven functioning in the event of a power outage.</p><p>One of the Haven's best features is a courtyard by landscape architecture firm Site Design Group and built on what was the Diplomat's south parking lot.</p><p>Residents can sit in colorful Adirondack chairs or table-and-chair sets. They can catch some shade beneath a minimalist pergola, or tend to the courtyard's herb garden.</p><p>Done-up in corals, blues and oranges, on a sunny day, the space looks like a slice of Southern California.</p><p>This is "trauma-informed design," which uses color, natural light, access to green space and soothing, textured surfaces to assist the healing process.</p><p>"This model was tested during COVID [and] it was successful, both at preventing transmittable diseases but also in improving mental health," Castañeda said. "When our mental health is at our best, it means that we can do our best in attaining permanent housing and all of those pieces."</p><p>Castañeda said the Department of Housing is looking to build more non-congregate shelters. </p><p>"It's important for us to continue to advance our vested interest in developing housing for all Chicagoans, regardless of income," she said.</p>

entries.title: Teen's body found shot, bound after mom gets call saying he was kidnapped in Greater Grand Crossing: report
entries.summary: <p>The mother of an 18-year-old man got a terrifying call from Venezuela: the caller said her son was kidnapped and told her where he was. On Tuesday night police found his body, according to a Chicago police report.</p><p>In a statement, police said they responded to a well being check about 9 p.m. Tuesday inside an apartment in the 6800 block of South Perry Avenue, where the unidentified teen, who suffered gunshot wounds to the chest and leg, was found and pronounced dead on the scene.</p><p>According to a police report, the teen's mother got a phone call from a person from Venezuela who she does not know. The caller told her that her son had been kidnapped about 3 p.m. Monday near a basketball court in the 7100 block of South King Drive and he could be found "inside an apartment" at the Perry Avenue address. </p><p>The teen was found lying face down in a bathtub with his hands tied behind his back, the report said. Three nine-millimeter shell casings were found near his body.</p><p>Area 1 detectives were investigating.<br></p>

Contributor Arionne Nettles, a South Side native with a defined accent of her own, answered the question in a<a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whljjc-l-yd/" target="_blank" > recently aired episode</a>.</p><p><b>Great Migration beginnings</b>: The answer goes back to the Great Migration, roughly between 1915 and 1970, during which a half-million Black people moved from Southern states to Chicago, creating a Black Chicago English you can hear in the dialect of their children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren.</p><p><b>Community connection</b>: Why the Southern accent has remained so prevalent in the city can be attributed to a few reasons, according to researcher Sharese King. Among them are Chicago's segregated communities and multiple generations living in the same neighborhood. Another reason is that many families are still connected with their southern kin. WBEZ’s sister station, refreshes lineup after almost shutting down</a></h3><p></p><h5>By <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whljjc-l-ti/" target="_blank" >Stefano Esposito</a></h5><p>Vocalo, the local music radio station that helped make Chance the Rapper and Vic Mensa household names, is launching a live call-in show in hopes of "shaping what comes next."</p><p>"The Vocalo Hotline," a weekly show debuting 8 p.m. May 29 on both WBEZ 91.5 FM and Vocalo 91.1 FM, is part of a major refresh for the music station, which has struggled in recent years to attract an audience and generate sufficient revenue to cover expenses.</p><p>The call-in show is part of WBEZ’s renewed focus on Chicago-based programming, which includes the morning shows "In the Loop" and "Say More."</p><p>"Hotline," hosted by Vocalo DJ Nudia Hernandez, is set to be a one-hour radio broadcast built around listener requests, shout-outs and conversation. </p><p>The show almost didn’t happen. Two years ago, facing a worsening financial situation, CPM announced plans to discontinue Vocalo broadcasts, part of a broader series of cuts at the news organization.</p><p>Now, with a new show ready to premiere at the end of the month, Vocalo's voice is growing again.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whljjc-l-td/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>Where in the city can you find the strongest Chicago accents?</b></p><p><a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" ><i>Reply to this email</i></a><i> (please include your first and last name). We may run your answer in a future newsletter or story.</i></p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whljjc-l-tk/" target="_blank" >Yesterday, we asked you</a>: How do you feel about entertainment venues asking audiences <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whljjc-l-tu/" target="_blank" >to check in their phones for a device-free experience</a>?</p><p>Here’s some of what you said…</p><p>"I’ll have to admit, it’s a bit challenging. Experienced this at a concert last fall – and found myself constantly reaching for my now 'phantom' phone in order to take a photo. Spent the first 30 minutes aggravated but finally settled in and was able to enjoy the concert. Lesson learned? It’s not the end of the world!" — <i>Derek D. Forest</i></p><p>"Restricting device use at live shows is perfectly sensible out of respect for the performers and others in the audience. They already do this at the comedy clubs in New York, even going as [far] as having guests remove smart watches. It forces us to be fully present for the experience." — <i>Christine Lopez </i></p><p>"I would love to!  Unfortunately, as the director of the Peoria International Airport, I have to be constantly available in case of emergency, so having my phone available is mandatory.  One day I’m going to chuck it into a lake!" — <i>Gene Olson</i></p><p>"As someone who occasionally acts onstage, I’d love to be guaranteed that nobody’s phone is going to interrupt the performance. As long as nobody accidentally, or on purpose, walks away with someone else’s device, that is." — <i>Paul Lockwood</i> </p><hr><p> <br>Thanks for reading the Sun-Times Morning Edition!<br>Got a story you think we missed? <a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >Email us here.</a></p><hr><p><b>Written and curated by</b>: Matt Moore<br><b>Editor</b>: Eydie Cubarrubia</p><hr><p><i>The Chicago Sun-Times is a nonprofit supported by readers like you. entries.title: Here’s your 2026 guide to farmers markets throughout Chicago
entries.summary:
Chicago has a wealth of farmers markets, but reliable information about them can be scattered across websites and social media. To help, this guide brings together the most current information for farmers markets throughout Chicago. (We broke out 54 suburban markets into its own guide for 2026.)

This list of farmers markets in the city is organized by area, then by day of the week, Monday through Sunday, and alphabetically by market. Each listing includes the 2026 hours and dates of operation, address, links to websites and social accounts, bells and whistles (such as live music and specialty vendors beyond farm produce), and whether the Illinois Link card is accepted. A paw emoji next to the name of a market means pets — dogs on leash is the usual policy — are welcome.

(Did we miss your favorite market? Let us know at farmers@wbez.org.)

entries.title: 'I don't have an answer': Natasha Cloud on her long wait in free agency
entries.summary: <p>When WNBA training camps opened this spring, veteran point guard Natasha Cloud was conspicuously absent. Many wondered: why was a two-time All-Defense selection and 2019 champion left unsigned for so long?</p><p>The speculation ranged. It was her activism. It was her age. It was the condensed nature of a free agency period that left some players on the outside looking in.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> ultimately <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/05/04/sky-sign-point-guard-natasha-cloud" >signed her to a one-year deal</a> the week of the season opener. Speaking to media Wednesday about her experience in free agency, Cloud said she doesn’t know why it took so long.</p><p>"Everyone wants me to have an answer," Cloud said. "I don't have an answer for why my situation was what it was."</p><p>Cloud, 34, admitted she felt anxious and fearful about being out of the league entirely. Given her resume and the fact that she still feels like she's in her prime, the uncertainty was jarring. Last season, Cloud started for the Liberty, averaging 10 points and five assists per game. She was happy in New York, but the franchise did not extend a return offer.</p><p>Liberty general manager Jonathan Kolb said parting ways with Cloud <a class="Link" href="https://nypost.com/2026/04/26/sports/liberty-gm-lauds-natasha-cloud-as-her-wnba-free-agency-lingers/" target="_blank" >“wasn’t about fit” or her activism, but rather a reflection of their specific free-agency targets and a condensed timeline.</a> He vouched for her as a teammate as a person.</p><p>Still, Cloud said she never felt like she got a real answer.</p><p>"I appreciate all the kind words said about me, but I still don't have an answer," Cloud said. "That's not my burden to carry or to stress about. I did everything I needed to do as a player, as a person in the community, and sometimes that isn't valued the way that it should be. So what you do is you pivot."</p><p>The pivot came with turbulence. Cloud said her previous agency released her just days before the draft on April 13. She ultimately signed with Fabio Jardine and First Pick Management, a move she credits with "saving the day."</p><p>She said she still doesn’t know if her activism kept certain teams at bay, and she made clear she's never going to change that part of herself.</p><p>But she did think the long wait showed growth — and gave her something to prove. </p><p>"I think everyone expected me to be 'crash-out Tash' and to be blunt and talk my sh— as I usually do, but there's growth here," Cloud said. "I've really worked on who I am as a human being. I've worked on my water as well as my fire and when to use it.</p><p>"So I changed my perspective of it. It wasn't 'woe is me,' it wasn't 'sad me.' It was, 'I'm going to work, and when I get that opportunity I'm going to come in and smack the sh— out of everybody.'"</p><p>Cloud is playing with that kind of energy in Chicago. She is averaging 8.3 points and 4.7 assists in 24 minutes per game. Her defense and leadership has been central to the team's 3-1 start. And her versatility will be key for an undersized roster that was just dealt a massive blow: <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/05/19/rickea-jacksons-hot-start-to-the-season-ends-with-a-torn-acl" >losing star forward Rickea Jackson to a season-ending ACL injury.</a></p><p>In Chicago, Cloud said she feels wanted, valued, and aligned with a group trying to rewrite its narrative—organization included.</p><p>"I will say Chicago has completely revamped," Cloud said. "I think they took all the sh— being said the last few years and they put their money where their mouth is and they invested into this thing completely. And to be here when it's being revamped is a meaningful feeling."</p><p>As for the lack of closure with New York, she's trying to make peace with it. </p><p>"Everyone here has been in a relationship where there's no closure and you just move on and you move forward and the next relationship is great," she said. "I'm in this next relationship and I'm loving life. That doesn't mean I still don't have a lot of love for Brooklyn."</p>

entries.title: DuPage County correctional officer accused of sharing child sexual abuse material
entries.summary: <p>A 32-year-old deputy with the DuPage County sheriff's office has been fired after being accused of possessing and disseminating child abuse material, officials said Wednesday. </p><p>Steven M. Simmons, of Lisle, appeared in court Wednesday, charged with multiple crimes regarding child sexual abuse material, according to a statement from the DuPage County sheriff's office, which said the office learned on Monday that the Illinois Attorney General's office was investigating Simmons. </p><p>At the conclusion of the court hearing, Simmons' employment with the sheriff's office was terminated, the statement said. </p><p>Investigators and police officers from the Lisle police department conducted a search of Simmons' home on Tuesday in the 5500 block of Lakeside Drive in Lisle and he was taken into custody after evidence of child sexual abuse material was found, according to officials.</p><p>"This case is part of Attorney General Kwame Raoul's ongoing work in collaboration with federal law enforcement agencies and local law enforcement officials throughout Illinois to apprehend offenders who download and trade child sexual abuse images online," a statement from Raoul's office said.</p><p>The crimes Simmons is accused of are each punishable by up to 15 years in prison, if convicted, Raoul's statement said.</p><p>Simmons is due back in court on June 15.</p>

entries.title: Green Day’s ‘American Idiot’ musical announced as part of Goodman Theatre’s 2026-27 season
entries.summary: <p>The Goodman Theatre announced Wednesday that its 2026-27 season will include two shows that had smash Broadway runs: "American Idiot," the musical created by the punk band Green Day, and "John Proctor Is the Villain."</p><p>The season begins in September and continues through August 2027. The season kicks off Sept. 5 with the monthlong world premiere of "The Attic: Things I've Seen While Lying on My Back" — a circus arts show by 7 Fingers, a Montreal-based company founded by seven artists who came up through Cirque du Soleil</p><p>"The show tells very human stories while doing things you look at and say 'That's not actually possible,'" said Goodman Artistic Director Susan V. Booth.</p><p>"American Idiot," which centers on three disaffected teens, will have a five-week run beginning in of 2027. </p><p>It became a stage hit in the 2000s when it "kind of shot out of a cannon," said Booth, who reflected on the selection process for this season's shows.</p><p>"We were all looking for ways to talk about the American moment we're in ... plays and musicals that resonate, that slam up against it in a way that opens people up and makes them talk," she said. "And with 'American Idiot' I kept waiting for the moment when the lyrics would feel dated, and they don't. If anything, they've gotten more urgent. It's Green Day at its absolute best, just a rager about what makes young people feel disenfranchised and what they do with that feeling, and we're in the thick of that right now."</p><p>The Tony award-winning musical was co-written by Green Day frontman Billie Joe Armstrong and features the band's music.</p><p>"John Proctor Is the Villain" will make its Chicago debut and run from Jan. 23 to Feb. 21. </p><p>Written by American playwright Kimberly Belflower during the height of the #MeToo movement, the play centers on a group of teen girls in a conservative Appalachian town who believe something horrible has happened and rush to judge a person without much due diligence.</p><p>The play riffs off Arthur Miller's "The Crucible" — a 1953 play set during the 1692 Salem witch trials that serves as an allegory for the McCarthy-era Red Scare in the 1950s, exploring themes of mass hysteria, social persecution, and the dangers of false accusations.</p><p>"'The Crucible' is one of those plays that pops up every time we're dealing with restrictions on speech or notions of fascism," Booth said. "It comes around every time our society feels like we're not responsibly embracing the rights we have."</p><p>"This play is about the cost of keeping quiet and speaking too loudly too quickly, and it just strikes a chord. We're all in the moment of 'I need to act, need to do something' and trying to figure out the right thing is to do," Booth said.</p><p>Sadie Sink, the "Stranger Things" actress who starred in the recent Broadway production of the play, will not be in the Goodman production. </p><p>Nearly all casting decisions for the upcoming season are yet to be made.</p><p>One exception is the casting of actor Tim Hopper to play Scrooge in the 49th annual production of "The Christmas Carol," which will run from Nov. 13 to Dec. 31.</p><p>Actor Christopher Donahue played it the past two seasons. Larry Yando played it for 15 seasons before him.</p><p>"When the opportunity comes to fill that role, you just want to get it absolutely right, and Tim Hopper is a longtime Steppenwolf member and there's a grit and honesty to him, and he will take on the role as if its a brand new play," said Booth, who took over as artistic director in 2022 Goodman after Robert Falls held the position for 35 years.</p>

entries.title: ‘Broadview 6’ judge orders feds to closed-door hearing over grand jury transcripts, just days before trial
entries.summary: <p>The judge presiding over the case against the remaining members of the “Broadview Six” demanded Wednesday that prosecutors involved in the redaction of controversial grand jury transcripts appear personally in her courtroom for a closed-door hearing Thursday.</p><p>The surprise order from U.S. District Judge April Perry demands the appearance of "any" assistant U.S. attorney "who participated in the decision to redact portions of the grand jury transcripts, whether on the trial team or at the supervisory level."</p><p>The judge also wrote that, "due to the anticipated discussion of grand jury materials," and in an effort to avoid tainting the jury pool, "the proceedings will be conducted under seal."</p><p>A spokesman for U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros' office could not immediately be reached. Grand jury proceedings are traditionally treated as sensitive and handled behind closed doors.</p><p>It's unclear what prompted Perry's order, but it seems like bad news for prosecutors <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/18/broadview-6-ice-midway-blitz-trump-deportation-kat-abughazaleh" target="_blank" >six days before trial</a> is set to begin. </p><p>Charged in the case are former congressional candidate Kat Abughazaleh, Oak Park village trustee Brian Straw, 45th Ward Democratic committeeperson Michael Rabbitt and Andre Martin, who served as a member of Abughazaleh’s campaign staff. Each is charged with a misdemeanor count of forcibly impeding a federal agent. Charges against two other people previously indicted in the case have been dismissed.</p><p>The transcripts in question have been <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/04/broadview-six-grand-jury-transcript-conspiracy" target="_blank" >a point of controversy for weeks</a>, ever since prosecutors announced their intention to drop a felony conspiracy charge previously leveled against the defendants. While that seemed to signal good news for the defendants, their attorneys suspected it was a ploy to avoid disclosing an unredacted version of the transcript to the judge.</p><p>Defense attorneys made a “narrow” request in early April to review only the portions of grand jury transcripts that showed how prosecutors explained the conspiracy law to the grand jury.</p><p>Alternatively, they suggested prosecutors turn transcripts over to Perry so the judge could conduct her own review. The judge agreed to give them a look, and prosecutors filed transcripts, under seal, of grand jury appearances from Oct. 9, Oct. 16 and Oct. 23.</p><p>The original indictment was handed up Oct. 23.</p><p>The feds filed the transcripts April 23. The next day, the judge entered an order scheduling a hearing April 29. She also told prosecutors “to bring to the hearing fully un-redacted versions of the transcripts [they had] filed under seal … as well as a copy of any presentation(s) or document(s) shown to the grand jurors summarizing the law.”</p><p>But moments into the April 29 hearing, Assistant U.S. Attorney William Hogan disclosed the feds' plan to drop the conspiracy charge and file a new charging document. Perry wound up denying the defense motion for grand jury transcripts as moot — and concluding there was no reason to read the transcripts. </p><p>Defense attorneys have continued to push for disclosure of the transcript in the weeks since, though. Straw attorney Chris Parente urged Perry on Monday simply to look at an unredacted version, arguing that prosecutors may be hiding something that "could have tainted all of this."</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/18/broadview-6-ice-midway-blitz-trump-deportation-kat-abughazaleh" target="_blank" >Perry agreed</a> after prosecutors said they had no objection. </p><p>In fact, prosecutors have accused defense attorneys of speculating "histrionically" about what might be in the transcript, insisting there was nothing "nefarious" about what happened.</p><p><i>This is a developing story. Check back for updates.</i></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/18/broadview-6-ice-midway-blitz-trump-deportation-kat-abughazaleh" target="_blank" >Trial nearing in case of remaining ‘Broadview 6' ICE protesters, who may be labeled members of a ‘mob’</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/04/29/broadview-ice-crime-chicago-trump-kat-abughezaleh" target="_blank" >Feds drop conspiracy charge against ‘Broadview Six’ ICE protesters, who still face trial for impeding officer</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/04/broadview-six-grand-jury-transcript-conspiracy" target="_blank" >Remaining ‘Broadview Six’ defendants move to disclose grand jury transcripts, drop conspiracy charges</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Pocos residentes de Chicago compran seguros contra inundaciones. ¿Deberían hacerlo?
entries.summary: <p>Menos del 1% de los residentes del Condado de Cook tienen seguro contra inundaciones.</p><p>Se espera que las tormentas intensas, en parte alimentadas por el cambio climático, empeoren en las próximas décadas. Las recientes lluvias fuertes plantean la cuestión de si los dueños de casa en Chicago están cubiertos por su póliza de seguro existente en caso de que se inunde su sótano.</p><p>La respuesta es probablemente no.</p><p>"La mayoría de la gente no sabe qué es lo que está cubierto y qué no", dijo Douglas Heller, director de seguros en la Consumer Federation of America.</p><div </div> </div><p></p><h3>¿Están aumentando las inundaciones?</h3><p>Las grandes tormentas eléctricas se están volviendo más frecuentes y descargan más lluvia en un tiempo más corto. Las calles y los alcantarillados locales en Chicago y en los suburbios del Condado de Cook no están diseñados para manejar tanta lluvia, y eso está enviando agua a las calles y a las casas.</p><p>Las inundaciones en los sótanos son crónicas y generalizadas, especialmente en comunidades de color de bajos ingresos, donde las calles y la infraestructura de alcantarillado obsoleta han recibido pocas mejoras y carecen de espacios verdes.</p><p>Las tormentas severas que causan inundaciones, granizo y tornados resultaron en pérdidas de $50 mil millones en Estados Unidos en cada uno de los últimos tres años, según el grupo de investigación de la industria, el Instituto de Información de Seguros.</p><h3>¿Cómo sé si necesito seguro contra inundaciones?</h3><p>Casi todas las comunidades del área de Chicago están en riesgo de inundación. Los alcantarillados del vecindario están diseñados para contener 2 pulgadas de lluvia en un período de 24 horas. Algunas tormentas están descargando cuatro veces esa cantidad. Lo mismo se aplica al Condado de Cook en los suburbios.</p><p>La lluvia cae de tal manera y con tanta rapidez que abruma los alcantarillados y no permite que el agua fluya a través de un enorme sistema de mitigación de inundaciones conocido como el <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2015/5/10/18451028/thornton-quarry-the-grand-canyon-of-the-south-suburbs-will-soon-be-underwater" target="_blank" >Deep Tunnel</a>.</p><p>Muchos dueños de casa están descubriendo que no cuentan con el seguro adecuado para cubrir las pérdidas por agua en sus casas.</p><h3>¿Cómo puedo averiguar si mi seguro de propietario cubre las inundaciones en el sótano?</h3><p>Los principales aseguradores, como State Farm y Allstate, no cubrirán automáticamente la inundación por el desborde de alcantarillado como parte de un plan regular de propietario.</p><p>Desde 1968, el gobierno federal ha sido el principal asegurador contra inundaciones en todo el país.</p><p>Allstate lo dice de forma contundente en su sitio web: “Ningún tipo de daño por inundación, sin importar la fuente del agua, está cubierto por las pólizas estándar de propietarios”.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" No fue así.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Giacomo Cain/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Larry Quinn Jr., que vive en el vecindario de Austin, pensó que su seguro de propietarios de State Farm cubriría las inundaciones. En 2023, más de cinco pies de agua inundaron su sótano a través de los desagües.</p><p>“El agua salía disparada por los alcantarillados. Literalmente salía en chorros”, dice Quinn.</p><p>El agua arruinó dos “boilers”, varios electrodomésticos, herramientas eléctricas grandes y una placa de circuito eléctrico, y hasta ahora le ha costado a Quinn unos $70,000 en daños. Su seguro no cubrió los costos de reparar ni de reemplazar nada, dice.</p><p>State Farm dice que alienta a la gente a revisar sus pólizas con sus agentes.</p><p>Esto es lo que debes buscar en tu póliza: Tu seguro de propietario enumerará una serie de "exclusiones", incluyendo el daño por agua. Necesitas preguntarle a tu agente sobre la cobertura adicional, a menudo denominada "anexo", que cubrirá el desborde del alcantarillado en el sótano que dañe artículos personales, así como cosas estructurales, como una caldera o “boiler”.</p><p>Es importante repasar múltiples escenarios con un asegurador o agente para asegurarte de que estás comprando el tipo de cobertura adecuada.</p><p>Por ejemplo: Pregunta “¿Estoy cubierto en caso de que el agua del alcantarillado se desborde en mi sótano?”</p><h3>Si mi asegurador no me ofrece un seguro contra inundaciones , ¿qué opciones tengo?</h3><p>El seguro adicional de empresas privadas puede costar varios cientos de dólares, pero el riesgo será un determinante clave para saber si incluso puedes comprar la cobertura. Asegúrate de entender por qué razones una póliza cubre el daño estructural o la propiedad personal.</p><p>El gobierno ofrece planes de seguro contra inundaciones para personas de áreas propensas a ellas a través del Programa Nacional de Seguro contra Inundaciones (NFIP). Pero el plan del gobierno federal, disponible para todos en Chicago y en gran parte del Condado de Cook, puede tener cobertura limitada para daños en el sótano. No cubrirá artículos personales guardados en un sótano ni ninguna remodelación realizada en un área.</p><p>El seguro federal contra inundaciones puede costar al menos $700 al año. Las cotizaciones estimadas pueden calcularse en <a class="Link" href="https://www.floodsmart.gov" target="_blank" >https://www.floodsmart.gov</a>. La propiedad puede asegurarse por hasta $250,000 dólares en daños.</p><p><i>Este artículo fue realizado como un proyecto para el Centro de Periodismo de Salud de USC Annenberg y el Centro de Periodismo y Comunicación de Clima 2025 de la Beca de Reporteo sobre Salud y Cambio Climático. </i></p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Trump orders banks to take a closer look at clients’ citizenship in new immigration enforcement move
entries.summary: <p>WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Tuesday signed an executive order that requires banks to take a closer look at the citizenship of their customers, a new measure in his administration’s push to clamp down on people living in the country illegally.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2026/05/restoring-integrity-to-americas-financial-system/" target="_blank" >order</a> directs bank regulators and government departments to look for signs that people without legal status are opening accounts or obtaining loans or credit cards. However, the order is less aggressive than banks had expected, as earlier reports suggested the White House was drafting an order that would make collecting customers’ citizenship information mandatory.</p><p>In the order, the White House framed the decision that banks would face credit risks if one of their customers were deported and any loans could no longer be repaid. The White House said it would not “permit risks to our financial system posed by the extension of credit or financial services to the inadmissible and removable alien population.”</p><p>Since banks have never collected any information about their customers’ citizenship or immigration status, there are no reliable public figures on how much risk these customers pose to the financial system.</p><p>A study by the left-leaning <a class="Link" href="https://www.urban.org/sites/default/files/2024-02/ITIN%20Mortgages.pdf" target="_blank" >Urban Institute</a> estimated that between 5,000 and 6,000 mortgages were issued to customers with Individual Taxpayer Identification Numbers (ITINs). These ITINs are typically used by undocumented workers in place of a Social Security Number. The Urban Institute estimated that banks were highly reluctant to lend to individuals with ITINs. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac are also generally reluctant to insure mortgages for borrowers with an ITIN, making it even less likely for ITIN holders to obtain a mortgage.</p><p>The White House has been signaling for weeks that it was planning some sort of executive order that would involve how banks handle their undocumented customers. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said last month that “there should be stricter rules” to open bank accounts.</p><p>“Why can the unknown foreign nationals come and open a bank account?” Bessent said.</p><p>Claiming bank executives were supposed to “know your customer,” he asked, “So how do you know your customer if you don’t know if they have legal or illegal status, whether a U.S. citizen or green card holder?”</p><p>In response, the banking industry had been aggressively lobbying for months to stop the White House from issuing an executive order that would have made collecting customers’ citizenship status mandatory, arguing it would be expensive and require vast amounts of paperwork. Since the order only offers guidance to the banks instead of a mandate, it appears the banks were able to win over the White House.</p><p>Immigration advocates have previously said any order that would order banks to collect citizenship information would likely result in undocumented immigrants moving out of the financial system, increasing the number of “unbanked” individuals.</p><p>The White House has taken other measures to discourage undocumented workers from using the financial system. The Treasury last November announced that it would reclassify certain refundable tax credits as “federal public benefits,” which bars some immigrant taxpayers from receiving them, even if they file and pay taxes and would otherwise qualify.</p><p>Tax experts said immigrants brought to the U.S. illegally by their parents as children, known as Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, or DACA, recipients, and immigrants with Temporary Protected Status would be largely affected by the planned change.</p>
entries.author: AP

entries.title: City Council approves compromise that freezes hourly pay for tipped workers
entries.summary: <p>Chicago restaurants fighting for survival amid rising food, labor and operating costs and the inflation-linked decline in their customer base got a temporary break Wednesday at the expense of their tipped employees.</p><p>The City Council agreed to freeze the hourly pay of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/05/12/subminimum-wage-phase-out-freeze-compromise-chicago-restaurants" >Chicago’s tipped workers</a> at 76% of the minimum wage for the next two years for large restaurants and for four more years for smaller establishments with 21 or fewer employees.</p><p>The compromise was hammered out by rookie Ald. Walter R. Burnett (27th) without Mayor Brandon Johnson’s involvement. The mayor must now decide whether to issue his fourth veto or risk the political embarrassment of an override.</p><p>Johnson used his <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/03/25/brandon-johnson-veto-freeze-subminimum-wage-phase-out-tipped-workers-restaurants" >third veto</a> to preserve one of the key items on his progressive to-do list and managed to make it stick. But with only one dissenting vote on Wednesday, the chances of a fourth veto succeeding appear slim. </p><p>The mayor is more likely to swallow hard and accept the compromise, just as both sides of the heated debate have reluctantly agreed to do.</p><p>If the remarks made Wednesday by one of the mayor's most powerful City Council allies are any indication, a fourth mayoral veto may be coming.</p><p>The lone "no" vote was cast by Budget Chair Jason Ervin (28th), who said freezing the wages of a workforce that includes the "poorest of the poor in Chicago" is an "economic betrayal and a moral failure."</p><p>"There's a difference between compromise and caving in," Ervin said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure What about their lights and their bills and their groceries?"</p><p>Far Southwest Side Ald. Matt O'Shea (19th) said a parade of restaurant owners in his border ward have told him they don't want to leave Beverly, but city mandates have them seriously considering moves to suburbs like Oak Lawn, Evergreen Park and Blue Island. </p><p>"If the restaurants don't exist or leave to go the suburbs, nobody's got jobs," O'Shea said.</p><p>The compromise did not satisfy either side of the debate, but both sides accepted it. </p><p>During the public comment period that preceded Wednesday’s City Council meeting, Illinois Restaurant Association President Sam Toia reiterated that the temporary freeze is “not the ideal outcome for our industry.”</p><p>But it’s “more workable and less harmful” to restaurants fighting to stay in business, particularly in wards that border suburbs.</p><p>“Operators need time to adjust so they can keep their doors open and their staff employed,” Toia said. “Predictability matters for workers, too. Abrupt changes can lead to reduced hours, fewer shifts, higher menu prices, more service charges and fewer opportunities for tipped employees.”</p><p>Saru Jayaraman of the One Fair Wage Coalition has also accepted the multiyear wage freeze for those she has called the “lowest-wage workforce in Chicago in the midst of the greatest cost of living increase in United States history.”</p><p>“If we are going to agree to this substitute, which we said we can live with, this has to be the end of the conversation. We should not have to continuously re-litigate something that the city has already agreed is the right thing to do, which is paying this lowest-wage workforce a full minimum wage with tips on top, like every other workforce in the city of Chicago,” Jayaraman said May 12. </p><p>Without the freeze, tipped workers now paid $12.62 an hour would receive a raise to 16% of Chicago’s minimum wage. That amount is reset every July 1 to match the cost of living. With the freeze, they would still receive a raise, but it would be capped at 76% of whatever the minimum hourly wage turns out to be.</p><p>Restaurants are mandated by law to make up the difference for servers whose hourly pay and tips do not equal the minimum wage.</p><h3>Sweepstakes machine ban vote delayed</h3><p>Johnson managed to avoid what might have been a second political defeat when Ald. Anthony Beale (9th) and Ald. Ray Lopez (15th) moved to postpone a vote that would have banned sweepstakes machines in Chicago,</p><p>Beale said he remains determined to maximize revenue from video gambling terminals by eliminating illegal competition from the 7,000 sweepstakes machines now operating illegally in Chicago. But he postponed a vote on the ban to beat Alds. Pat Dowell (3rd) and Nicole Lee (11th) to the punch. </p><p>"All I’m trying to do is maximize the money we can from VGTs," Beale said. The commissioner has voiced concern that the regulations that Beale proposed may be “overly broad and burdensome” and have a “disparate impact on various communities.”</p><p></p><p>Sweepstakes gambling machines look like video slot machines but have managed to operate in a gray area of the law by offering “free play” options and coupons to winners instead of cash.</p><h3>EV parking spaces pilot ordinance</h3><p>Also on Wednesday, Johnson introduced an ordinance that would authorize Transportation Commissioner William Cheaks Jr. to designate parking spaces “on the public way or in any public or private parking facility” for the “exclusive use of electric vehicles charging at an electric vehicle charging station.”</p><p>The “Electric Curbside Charging Pilot” would terminate June 30, 2030. Cheaks would be empowered to “install, operate and maintain” those charging stations or “enter into agreements” with private entities to create those stations. Motorists parking in those designated spaces would face $100 fines.</p>

entries.title: City Council approves $54.7M tax break to jump-start United Center development
entries.summary: <p>The City Council on Wednesday approved a $54.7 million<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/05/11/city-council-economic-development-committee-tax-breaks-united-center-entertainment-district" > property tax break </a>that developers say is critical to secure financing for their $7 billion plan to turn a sea of parking lots around the United Center into a massive residential and entertainment complex.</p><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson has defended the United Center subsidy even though he’s trying to block a separate property tax break that could pave the way for the Bears move to Arlington Heights by arguing that owners of billion-dollar sports franchises shouldn’t receive handouts.</p><p>The City Council overwhelmingly agreed — even though the 12-year $54.7 million Class B property tax cut only applies to Phase One of the $7 billion development.</p><p>The Wirtz and Reinsdorf families, owners of the United Center and the Bulls and Blackhawks, have not ruled out seeking additional property tax breaks for subsequent phases. </p><p>Tens of millions in public funding may also be required to build a new Pink Line CTA station near the United Center. Specifics of that project have not finalized.</p><p>Steve Rucks, chief financial officer of the United Center, told a City Council committee earlier this month that it’s been a struggle to nail down the remaining 80% of private financing to bankroll the $500 million first phase of the project “with the market where it is today and construction costs where they are.”</p><p>That private financing is contingent upon City Council approval of the property tax break, Rucks said.</p><p> Ald. Walter R. Burnett (27th) has hailed the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2024/07/23/united-center-reinsdorf-wirtz-1901-project-housing-entertainment-hall-retail-campus-arena" target="_blank" >1901 Project</a> as the largest investment on the Near West Side since the United Center was built more than 30 years ago under his father’s tenure as 27th Ward alderman.</p><p>Burnett has predicted that, even with the tax break, the project will be a catalyst for growth on the Near West Side and beyond, generating millions of dollars in new development and tax revenue for the city.</p><p>Phase 1 of the 1901 project will be anchored by a 6,000-seat music hall, and will include a public plaza, boutique hotel and parking deck with a rooftop park.</p><p>The 800,000 square feet of development is expected to generate $46.3 million more in tax revenue and create nearly 2,000 construction jobs, 600 permanent jobs and 180 part-time positions.</p><p></p><p>Developers' 2014 zoning application called for up to 9,463 residential units, 20% of them affordable; and 1,309 hotel rooms. The height of the tallest building t would be 660 feet, making it the tallest building in the surrounding area.</p><p>The 6,000 seat music hall and other entertainment-related uses at Damen and Adams would fill a void on a Chicago music scene that now includes small and large venues, but nothing in between.</p><p>A parking deck topped by a 2.5-acre park is part of Phase One. The entire project would include roughly ten acres of new green space, if developers proceed with all seven phases.</p><p>Burnett’s father, retired Ald. Walter Burnett Jr. was enticed by the increase in affordable units, which would include student housing for nearby Malcolm X College.</p><p>“I love the green space. I love the skating rink. I love the retail. I love the fact that the United Center is working with the community with some of their retail spaces," the elder Burnett told the Sun-Times when the zoning application was introduced.</p><p>The initial filing made no mention of the CTA station that developers believe is need to access the planned residential and entertainment district and minimize the need for parking.</p><p>But the elder Burnett said nearly two years ago that the new Pink Line station was under discussion and that a likely funding source would be the surrounding tax increment financing district, though the TIF “may be expiring.”</p><p>Further complicating matters is Mayor Brandon Johnson’s $1.25 billion bond issue to bankroll affordable housing and economic development projects. It weans the city off of its longstanding dependence on TIFs.</p><p></p>
entries.author: Fran Spielman

entries.title: La meta del brasileño de correr en todas las calles de Chicago continúa luego de un susto con su visa
entries.summary: <p>Cuando Joabe Barbosa se propuso correr por todas las calles de Chicago, no sabía cuánto tiempo le permitirían quedarse en los Estados Unidos.</p><p>Ahora, mientras el estudiante de posgrado de la Universidad Roosevelt se prepara para completar su travesía el próximo mes, lo hace sabiendo que Chicago seguirá siendo su hogar.</p><p>Hace dos semanas, Barbosa descubrió que podría quedarse hasta 2028 después de que la Universidad Roosevelt gestionara que pudiera enseñar clases de pregrado mientras continuaba con su curso. Esto fue después de una avalancha de apoyo de los miles de seguidores que siguieron su recorrido por las calles de Chicago.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-eb0000" name="module-eb0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Y vino con algunas propuestas. Mientras su futuro en Chicago seguía siendo incierto, Barbosa comentó que su bandeja de entrada estaba inundada de cerca de 500 propuestas de matrimonio y varias ofertas de adopción.</p><p>Pero su madre se negó, dijo riendo.</p><p>"La gente de Chicago fue definitivamente muy útil al ofrecerme tantas oportunidades. Y solo saber que, si no funcionaba, tenía a tantas personas en quienes depender", comentó Barbosa.</p><p>Barbosa, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/04/02/brasileno-que-ha-corrido-por-las-calles-de-chicago-enfrenta-la-expiracion-de-su-visa-de-estudiante" target="_blank" >un brasileño que creció en Londres</a>, se mudó a Chicago en 2022 con una visa F-1 para cursar un doctorado en psicología clínica en la Universidad Roosevelt. Pero después de no haber encontrado pasantía durante su último año, Barbosa enfrentó la posibilidad de verse obligado a regresar a Brasil.</p><p>Desde entonces, Barbosa ha seguido corriendo por las calles de Chicago durante más de 400 días, ganando más de 50,000 seguidores en TikTok e Instagram.</p><p>"No los conté, pero probablemente tengo a alguien de cada uno de los vecindarios de Chicago con quien podría quedarme un año gratis", dijo.</p><p>Barbosa comentó que la universidad le ofreció apoyo financiero, lo que aligeró la carga para su familia y le permitió continuar sus estudios. Como estudiante internacional, dijo que su familia ha contraído deudas para ayudarlo a cubrir los costos de su educación.</p><p>El 14 de junio, hará su última carrera por Michigan Avenue desde Oak Street hasta Ida B. Wells Drive.</p><p>A pesar de no ser estadounidense, Barbosa dijo que Chicago se ha convertido en su hogar.</p><p>"Realmente, después de esta última vuelta, se mostrará cuánto amor y cuánta comunidad hay para la gente aquí y cuánto amor hay para las personas que realmente aman a Chicago", comentó.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Bears rival Aaron Rodgers says he will retire after the 2026 NFL season
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="aaron" target="_blank" >Bears</a> may have finally seen the last of quarterback Aaron Rodgers.</p><p>The Steelers quarterback claimed Wednesday he plans to retire at the end of the 2026 season. </p><p>“Yes,” he told Pittsburgh reporters. “This is it.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">"This is it."<br><br>Aaron Rodgers says he will retire after the 2026 season. <a href="https://t.co/mjPADJdRLY">pic.twitter.com/mjPADJdRLY</a></p>— SportsCenter (@SportsCenter) <a href="https://twitter.com/SportsCenter/status/2057169678925996379?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">May 20, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>If so, the only way he can face the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/05/18/bears-nfl-stadium-sites-arlington-heights-hammond-not-hammond-nfl-quarterly-meeting-orlando-tuesday" target="_blank" >Bears</a> again is if the two teams meet in the Super Bowl. The Bears played the Steelers last season, but Rodgers missed that game — his only absence of the year — with an injured left wrist. </p><p>Last week, Rodgers agreed to a $25 million deal to return to Pittsburgh for his second season there after playing two with the Jets. He cited a desire to play for new Steelers coach Mike McCarthy, his former boss with the Packers.</p><p>The two teamed up to win Super Bowl XLV with the Packers, the only title for either man. Rodgers spent 18 years in Green Bay, emerging as one of the most hated rivals in Chicago sports history. He dominated the Bears throughout his career, once claiming — with little pushback — that he owned them. Rodgers won four MVP awards and went to 10 Pro Bowls with the Packers.</p><p>Rodgers hinted he would retire last year, too, before returning to the Steelers.<br></p>

entries.title: Missed opportunities loom large as White Sox drop rubber match in Seattle
entries.summary: <p>SEATTLE — The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a>’ latest comeback effort fell short in Seattle on Wednesday as they left nine runners on base en route to a 5-4 loss to drop the rubber match of their three-game set against the Mariners.</p><p>Randal Grichuk’s pinch-hit home run heralded a potential dramatic rally in the ninth inning for the second time in as many games, but they couldn't muster another off Seattle reliever Jose Ferrer.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Randal Grichuk goes yard! <a href="https://t.co/qruNzTap0N">pic.twitter.com/qruNzTap0N</a></p>— Chicago White Sox (@whitesox) <a href="https://twitter.com/whitesox/status/2057232668270469299?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">May 20, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Earlier, the Sox drew three straight walks to load the bases in the second inning against Mariners’ starter Emerson Hancock, but he struck out Tristan Peters and got Drew Romo to ground into a double play to end the threat.</p><p>Sox starter Sean Burke hit Randy Arozarena with a pitch in the second inning, and the M’s outfielder scored on Dominic Canzone’s double.</p><p>Rookie Sam Antonacci responded as he singled, stole second and came home on Andrew Benintendi’s two-out single to tie the game in the third.</p><p>Arozarena walked to open the bottom of the fourth, stole second and came home on Patrick Wisdom’s double. Arozarena’s steal looked like it might have been worth a review, but umpires said Sox shortstop Luisangel Acuna blocked the base.</p><p>Three straight singles capped by Munetaka Murakami’s RBI knotted the game for the Sox in the fifth.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Mune comes through 💪<br><br>His 33rd RBI of the season evens the score at 2 in the 5th <a href="https://t.co/jTohIdLdDi">pic.twitter.com/jTohIdLdDi</a></p>— White Sox on CHSN (@CHSN_WhiteSox) <a href="https://twitter.com/CHSN_WhiteSox/status/2057211983741514011?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">May 20, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The M’s loaded the bases with no outs in the fifth off Burke. Antonacci made a sliding catch on shallow fly. Arozarena popped out before manager Will Venable called in reliever Sean Newcomb, who drew a groundout to escape the jam.</p><p>Burke gave up two runs on four hits, three walks and two hit batters over 4 ⅔ innings, along with five strikeouts.</p><p>The Sox had runners on second and third in the sixth inning, but Seattle catcher Jhonny Pereda caught Chase Meidroth lingering off third on a bunt attempt by Romo, who then grounded out to end the threat..</p><p>Pereda took Newcomb deep to put the Mariners ahead with a solo home run in the bottom of the seventh, and Arozarena piled on with a two-run blast later in the inning off reliever Jordan Hicks.</p><p>The Sox got one back in the eighth with two runners on when Peters hit a would-be double-play grounder. Mariners’ shortstop Colt Emerson threw the relay wide to first and Meidroth scored on the error.</p><p>It was a tough day for Emerson, Seattle’s prized rookie, who got picked off first by Sox reliever Brandon Eisert to end the eighth inning.</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a
