entries.title: Thousands of Zillow listings in Chicago have vanished. Here's why
entries.summary: <p>Potential buyers browsing Zillow or Trulia for homes in the Chicago area have likely noticed significantly fewer listings.</p><p>That’s because the real estate company Zillow Group lost access Wednesday to thousands of property listings for its two websites, in the latest escalation of a legal battle with Lisle-based Midwest Real Estate Data. </p><p>The fight is over MRED's private listing network, where homes for sale are shared among real estate professionals. And MRED followed through on a threat to cut Zillow's access to its listing data feed. </p><p>There were nearly 5,000 Chicago homes listed on Zillow Tuesday, but as of Wednesday afternoon, that number plummeted to about 1,700. Meanwhile, other listing sites like Redfin and Realtor.com show about 5,000 to 8,000 listings in Chicago.</p><p>MRED manages listings — submitted by brokers — throughout Illinois, as well as parts of Wisconsin and Indiana. The regional multiple listing service has more than 43,000 members and processed more than 264,000 listings worth $43 billion in 2025.</p><p>The loss of listings on Zillow's websites have made a behind-the-scenes real estate industry fight public. And it nowhinders some consumers in their <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/01/30/affordability-chicago-housing-market-homebuyers-experts-economists" target="_blank" >search to buy a home</a>, while also limiting the marketing opportunity for sellers.</p><h3>Why is the cut off happening?</h3><p>In April 2025, Zillow implemented new standards around what homes could appear on its websites.</p><p>The changes stipulated that homes marketed to buyers behind a paywall or login portal were not eligible to appear on Zillow because they're private. Private listings, or so-called pocket listings, are commonplace in real estate. It's often done for celebrities or prominent figures who may not want everyone knowing their pricey mansion is on the market.</p><p>Zillow said the change was designed to protect transparency and encourage a competitive market.</p><p>MRED announced in April that it was expanding its long-time private listing network nationwide, and New York-based brokerage Compass would feed its listings to MRED, including private listings.</p><p>MRED said in a news release at the time that it would “protect and safeguard agents” using its private listing network from being banned or penalized by feed recipients like Zillow.</p><p>The move pushed Zillow to sue MRED and Compass last week, accusing the two of violating federal antitrust law by conspiring to hide home listings from potential buyers. The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois, also said the deal creates a monopoly where buyers and sellers will only want to work with Compass agents.</p><p>Compass has become Chicago’s largest brokerage firm. It acquired Chicago agency <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2024/12/03/real-estate-giant-compass-acquires-chicago-properties-christies-444m-deal" >@properties Christie’s International Real Estate</a> in December 2024, and, more recently, Anywhere Real Estate in January. Anywhere’s brands include Coldwell Banker, Century 21, Corcoran and Sotheby's International Realty.</p><h3>What do MRED and Compass say?</h3><p>Compass argues buyers have a right to market their property however they see fit. The brokerage said its partnership with MRED will give homeowners more choices and create a more competitive marketplace.</p><p>“Zillow is punishing agents for merely following their clients’ lawful instructions on how they want their homes marketed,” a Compass spokesperson said in a statement.</p><p>MRED had said Monday that it would suspend its feed of listing data to Zillow unless the company corrected a violation of its license agreements and MRED’s rules, which involved the refusal to display nine listings. The National Association of Realtors has longstanding rules that listing feeds like Zillow can’t filter out properties based on the agent or brokerage name. Compass said Zillow's new policy does this by removing Compass' listings from MRED.</p><p>"The rules of this MLS exist to protect every participating broker and every consumer who relies on a complete and accurate picture of the market," Rebecca Jensen, president and CEO of MRED, said. "Those rules apply equally to every participant, regardless of the size of their audience or the reach of their platform. MRED enforces its rules consistently and fairly, and hopes that Zillow returns to operating consistent with its longstanding agreements with MRED."</p><p>And MRED made good on its promise to cut off Zillow's access. It means no new MRED listings will populate on Zillow. A Zillow spokesperson said the company worked Wednesday morning to also remove existing MRED listings.</p><p>"In a striking lesson in irony, Zillow has chosen not to display 43,000 MRED listings because it demands the right, and has filed a federal antitrust lawsuit to secure that right — to exclude nine listings it disfavors," MRED said in a Wednesday news release.</p><p>The nine listings that violate its policies are private Compass listings in California, Florida and Georgia — all outside of MRED's traditional operating area. Zillow said the number of violating listings will balloon from nine if it changes its policy for MRED.</p><p>“The people paying the price today are real. Sellers who listed their homes expecting to reach every buyer on Zillow. Buyers who just want to see every home available to them. Thousands of independent agents who had no voice in this decision and nothing to gain from it. MRED sacrificed them all to protect the hidden listing scheme of the largest brokerage in the country,” a Zillow spokesperson said in a statement.</p>

entries.title: City Council votes to ban cops tied to far-right groups
entries.summary: <p>The City Council moved Wednesday to ban cops with ties to extremist groups like the far-right Proud Boys or Oath Keepers from serving in the Chicago Police Department.</p><p>The ordinance from Ald. Matt Martin (47th) prohibits officers from engaging in “extremist activities,” defined in the measure as any attempt to overthrow the U.S. government through violence or “unconstitutional means.” The measure also bans police from actively participating in extremist groups, such as doing fundraising, recruiting or displaying tattoos to uplift extremist groups.</p><p>It passed 28-21.</p><p>Under the new ordinance, alleged extremist activities or ties to extremist groups will be investigated by the Civilian Office of Police Accountability, an independent city watchdog, instead of the department’s internal investigatory unit.</p><p>In his appeal to colleagues, Martin said Chicago must defend against federal acts such as President Donald Trump’s Day 1 signing of roughly 1,500 pardons and commutations for those convicted of attacking the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021. Martin added that the ordinance protects against extremism beyond Trump’s presidency.</p><p>“These definitions [of extremism] are content-neutral, meaning that they give no weight whatsoever to someone’s political leanings,” Martin said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-780000" name="image-780000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3c9c804/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6887x3865+0+364/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F4c%2F49%2Ff7fe7cbf4ebcb30f4c42b0ac2f66%2Fcouncil-260521-35-martin.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/885cf91/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6887x3865+0+364/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F4c%2F49%2Ff7fe7cbf4ebcb30f4c42b0ac2f66%2Fcouncil-260521-35-martin.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3ed9db2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6887x3865+0+364/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F4c%2F49%2Ff7fe7cbf4ebcb30f4c42b0ac2f66%2Fcouncil-260521-35-martin.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Ald. Matt Martin (47th), shown speaking at Wednesday’s City Council meeting, sponsored an ordinance that prohibits police officers with ties to far-right groups. The ordinance passed the Council 28-21.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Martin cited a 2024 report from city Inspector General Deborah Witzburg, which stated “the city’s handling of extremism in its police ranks has fallen short.”</p><p>At least a dozen Chicago police officials were previously investigated for their alleged ties to the Oath Keepers and Proud Boys, extremist groups whose members played a key role in the Jan. 6 riot.</p><p>The measure follows a joint investigation by the Chicago Sun-Times and WBEZ, called “Extremism in the Ranks,” which documented troubling allegations against Chicago cops on a leaked roster of an anti-government group and the efforts to hold those officers accountable.</p><p>The ordinance passed after a heated debate in which some of the Council’s conservative and moderate members argued the ordinance will discourage Chicagoans from joining the police department because it singles out officers.</p><p>“Hell yeah, go after the white supremacists, hell yeah! But go after them in every department,” said Ald. Anthony Napolitano (41st), a former police officer, who claimed the ordinance “once again demonizes” cops. Council members who support the ordinance, he said, “want to destroy that department.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-770000" name="image-770000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5e0ee39/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7088x3978+0+375/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8a%2Ffb%2Ffd3c5df043a2a2c6f532f2e6d455%2Fcouncil-260521-33-napolitano.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e165e95/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7088x3978+0+375/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8a%2Ffb%2Ffd3c5df043a2a2c6f532f2e6d455%2Fcouncil-260521-33-napolitano.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d8e77cd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7088x3978+0+375/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8a%2Ffb%2Ffd3c5df043a2a2c6f532f2e6d455%2Fcouncil-260521-33-napolitano.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Ald. Anthony Napolitano (41st) speaks during a Chicago City Council meeting at City Hall, Wednesday, May 20, 2026." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d8e77cd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7088x3978+0+375/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8a%2Ffb%2Ffd3c5df043a2a2c6f532f2e6d455%2Fcouncil-260521-33-napolitano.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a79c242/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7088x3978+0+375/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8a%2Ffb%2Ffd3c5df043a2a2c6f532f2e6d455%2Fcouncil-260521-33-napolitano.JPG 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d8e77cd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7088x3978+0+375/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8a%2Ffb%2Ffd3c5df043a2a2c6f532f2e6d455%2Fcouncil-260521-33-napolitano.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Ald. Anthony Napolitano (41st) opposed an ordinance backed by Ald. Matt Martin to prohibit police officers from maintaining ties with far-right groups. Napolitano, a former police officer, said the ban should cover all city employees, instead of singling out police officers.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Ald. Demon Yancy (5th), who calls himself a “cop kid” because his dad served in CPD, clapped back, saying it’s “way past ridiculous” to debate “whether racism exists and … whether it exists in the police department.”</p><p>“We talk about the role of police being the thin blue line. … When the ‘thin blue line' includes bad guys, it makes it really hard to think about how we mend the relationship between police and community,” Yancy said.</p><p>An earlier version of the ordinance applied the ban on extremist activity to all city employees, but it was narrowed to avoid court challenges, Martin said.</p><p>Martin told colleagues when it comes to police officers, courts have offered “more leeway” to prohibit extremist activity “because of the unique role they play in public safety.”</p><p>The more narrow scope also eased concerns from progressive advocates that the law could be used to tamp down on constitutional political activism in the future.</p><p>“We are concerned that in this political climate, designations like ‘anti-government extremists’ can be applied broadly, sweeping up those working tirelessly to protect our neighbors and our democracy,” Loren Jones, with the policy nonprofit, Impact for Equity, said at a committee hearing last month.</p><p>But the fact that “this ordinance applies only to the Chicago Police Department” lessens that concern, she said.</p><p>Ald. Chris Taliaferro, who chairs the Council’s police and fire committee, moved to delay the ordinance’s passage and re-refer it to his committee, after expressing frustration that the measure had been heard only in the Council’s Workforce Development Committee.<br></p>

entries.title: Waiting game getting old for injured White Sox catcher Kyle Teel
entries.summary: <p>SEATTLE — Ailing <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox</u></a> catcher Kyle Teel is learning lessons he’d rather not have to sit through as he tries to work his way back to MLB action for the first time this season.</p><p>“This is the first time I’ve been injured in my career,” a frustrated Teel said after meeting his teammates in Seattle following <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/05/18/kyle-teel-injury-knee-white-sox" >the knee injury</a> that derailed his rehab assignment from a pulled hamstring. “I’m learning as I go throughout this process.</p><p>“Patience is important. At the same time, being impatient in a way that’s trying to get back as fast as I can. So it’s the combo of those two variables,” he said.</p><p>On the cusp of his big-league return from the hammy pulled during the World Baseball Classic, Teel’s cleat got caught in the batter’s box while swinging at Triple-A Charlotte over the weekend. It sprained a ligament in his right knee, setting him back an estimated three to six weeks.</p><p>The prized backstop is taking solace in joining the chorus of recuperating Sox cheerleaders traveling with the team, including Mike Vasil (Tommy John surgery) and Tanner Murray (fractured shoulder).</p><p>“I love these guys,” Teel said. “We have an unbelievable team and I’m so grateful to be a part of it in any way I can… I want to bring energy to the clubhouse, I want to bring energy during the games. And then when it’s time to go, I want to go and give it my all.”</p><h3>Sigh of relief</h3><p>Third baseman Miguel Vargas was out of the starting lineup but entered Wednesday's game from the bench a day after getting plunked with a pitch to the right hand <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/05/19/white-sox-mariners-rally-meidroth-benintendi" >in Tuesday’s 2-1 win</a>. X-rays revealed no structural damage.</p><p>“I definitely thought it would be worse in the moment,” Vargas said. “I was praying for that. I feel good today.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-c40000" name="image-c40000"></a> Perry</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-0f844980-525d-11f1-8545-afce7e092f61"><li>Fleetwood-Jourdain Theatre presents <b>“Gee’s Bend,”</b> Elyzabeth Gregory Wilder’s play that follows a family from 1939-2002 as they experience segregation, family strife, the Civil Rights Movement and celebrity. The play is set in the real-life Alabama community of Gee’s Bend, which has become known for the hand-stitched quilts made by generations of women who grew up there. Tim Rhoze directs. From May 23-June 7 at Noyes Cultural Arts Center, 927 Noyes St., Evanston. Tickets: $33. Visit <a class="Link" href="http://fjtheatre.com" target="_blank" ><u>fjtheatre.com</u></a>.</li><li>Blue Demon Theatre stages <b>“Company,”</b> Stephen Sondheim and George Furth’s musical comedy about a man who contemplates his single life leading him to examine marriage, his relationships and his life. Sydney Sallman directs. From May 22-24 at Greenhouse Theater, 2257 N. Lincoln Ave. Tickets: $11, $22. Visit <a class="Link" href="http://greenhousetheater.org" target="_blank" ><u>greenhousetheater.org</u></a>.</li><li>Boston-based Cunning Folk Theatre comes to town with its production of <b>“Stories,”</b> which follows a young Jewish storyteller in 1898 Warsaw as he tries to write a story that will intrigue a woman who he is definitely (he tells himself) not in love with. From May 27-31 at Athenaeum Center, 2936 N. Southport Ave. Tickets: $24, $29. Visit <a class="Link" href="http://athenaeumcenter.org" target="_blank" ><u>athenaeumcenter.org</u></a>.</li></ul><h3><b>Dance</b></h3><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-0f844981-525d-11f1-8545-afce7e092f61"><li>Chicago Movement Collective and Winifred Haun & Dancers present <b>“Persistent Spring,”</b> an annual event showcasing new works by Rachel Walker, Steven Hou, Imani English, Faith von Atzigen, Winifred Haun, Valerie Lowder and more. At 7 p.m. May 22 at Ruth Page Center for the Arts, 1016 N. Dearborn St. Tickets: $39. entries.title: Trump administration gives Illinois nearly $300 million to replace toxic lead pipes
entries.summary: <p><i>This coverage is made possible through a partnership between WBEZ and </i><a class="Link" href="http://grist.org/" target="_blank" ><i>Grist</i></a><i>, a nonprofit environmental media organization.</i></p><p>Illinois is receiving nearly $300 million in federal funding to track down and replace toxic lead pipes that deliver drinking water to homes across the state.</p><p>The major investment is part of a $2.9 billion national funding package from the Trump administration’s Environmental Protection Agency.</p><p>Illinois received about 10% of the federal dollars — the largest allocation among all 50 states.</p><p>Nationwide, the EPA estimates there are approximately 4 million lead service lines buried across the country that are still in use. Illinois leads the nation, with about <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/environment/2026/03/23/can-replacing-illinois-toxic-lead-pipes-create-more-jobs" target="_blank" ><u>1.5 million lead pipes</u></a>. More than 400,000 of the state's lead service lines are in Chicago as a result of the city’s building codes which required lead connections up until 1986.</p><p>There is no safe level of lead exposure according to the EPA. Lead is a potent neurotoxin that can cause irreversible cognitive, cardiovascular and reproductive problems. Plumbing containing lead is dangerous because it can leach into drinking water and has no smell or taste.</p><p>“[We] will work hard to secure our fair share but there is no determination yet about how much Chicago will receive,” according to a statement from Megan Vidis, spokesperson for the Chicago Department of Water Management.</p><p>The Trump administration is branding the investment as part of its “Make America Healthy Again” initiative, but the funds were previously promised under the Biden-era Bipartisan Infrastructure Law. The investment was slashed earlier this year when Republican lawmakers repurposed <a class="Link" href="https://insideclimatenews.org/news/12012026/congress-may-cut-lead-pipe-replacement-funding/" target="_blank" ><u>$125 million</u></a> from the funding package for wildfire prevention.</p><p>Due to the cut, Illinois will receive approximately $15 million less than it would have originally.</p><p>"If the federal government is serious about getting the lead out and modernizing the nation’s aging water infrastructure, then it must sustain Bipartisan Infrastructure Law investments and be committed to strengthening, not scaling back,” said Chakena Sims, a senior policy advocate with the Natural Resources Defense Council.</p>

entries.title: Juez ordena la liberación de una mamá de CPS detenida por ICE; su hijo adolescente sigue detenido
entries.summary: <p>Se ordenó la liberación de la madre de un estudiante de 18 años de la secundaria Mather de la custodia migratoria por un juez federal el martes, aunque el adolescente sigue detenido, según los abogados de la familia.</p><p>Ricardo Navarrete y su madre, Liliana Navarrete, fueron <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/04/21/comunidad-escolar-y-de-futbol-queda-conmocionada-tras-detencion-de-estudiante-y-su-mama-por-ice" target="_blank" >detenidos por agentes federales en marzo</a> durante una audiencia judicial rutinaria en su caso de asilo. Madre e hijo llegaron a Chicago en 2022 como solicitantes de asilo procedentes de Colombia.</p><p>Liliana Navarrete fue una de las 18 personas liberadas mediante un decreto de <a class="Link" href="https://joannaklonsky.us3.list-manage.com/track/click?u=5d5e50872dd1af3b8172cf48b&id=674152938f&e=a34e5536a9" target="_blank" >hábeas corpus</a> por un juez de distrito en Kentucky después de haber sido detenida durante demasiado tiempo sin una audiencia de fianza, según un comunicado de sus abogados. La lucha por su caso migratorio continuará en la corte mientras regresa a Chicago.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-510000" name="module-510000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>El adolescente, que anteriormente describió haber estado encerrado en cuartos estrechos con docenas de hombres, sigue en custodia.</p><p>“Liliana puede regresar a su hogar en Chicago, Illinois y continuar con su caso ante la corte de inmigración de Chicago”, dijo Kelli Fennell, una abogada que representa a la familia, en un comunicado. “Su familia y comunidad tienen la esperanza de que pronto recibirán una decisión positiva respecto a su hábeas pendiente”.</p><p>Un destacado jugador de fútbol, Ricardo firmó para jugar con la poderosa institución de fútbol, Truman College, después de graduarse. Esos planes son inciertos dada su detención actual.</p><p>Kristy Morrow, una amiga de la familia que ha estado apoyándolos, tenía esperanzas para el caso de Liliana, ya que su distrito judicial en Kentucky ha estado otorgando peticiones de hábeas.</p><p>Morrow espera que la petición de hábeas de Ricardo también pueda ser concedida tras una decisión de la corte de apelaciones federal de la semana pasada. La decisión establece que los detenidos migratorios no pueden permanecer detenidos sin una audiencia de fianza.</p><p>Ricardo le ha dicho a su familia que lo mantienen en una cárcel del condado, junto con otros 90 hombres. Las luces permanecen encendidas toda la noche y hay ruido constante, dijo Morrow.</p><p>“Tenemos un muchacho que se está perdiendo el baile de prom, la graduación y su última temporada de fútbol”, dijo Morrow. “Necesitamos traer a este chico a casa”.</p><p>Ricardo se perderá el resto de la temporada de su club de fútbol, que termina el sábado, mucho antes de su próxima fecha de corte en julio.</p><p>Pero el equipo lo ha mantenido en la lista, dijo Morrow. Y su nombre es mencionado en cada partido por el árbitro.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/04/21/comunidad-escolar-y-de-futbol-queda-conmocionada-tras-detencion-de-estudiante-y-su-mama-por-ice" target="_blank" >Los partidarios se manifestaron el mes pasado por Ricardo y su madre</a>, pidiendo su liberación y el fin de la campaña de deportaciones de la administración de Trump desde el final del Operativo Midway Blitz en el área de Chicago.</p><p>“Todos son estudiantes de último año, así que es agridulce”, dijo. “Han tenido una gran temporada, pero se dan cuenta de lo que está sucediendo y de la gravedad de esto. Su compañero de equipo está ausente”.</p><p><i>Contribuyó: Emmanuel Camarillo </i></p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>
